name: Chapter 3: Current Electricity
description: Current, Ohm’s law, drift velocity, mobility, resistivity and temperature, power, emf and internal resistance, cells, Kirchhoff’s rules, Wheatstone bridge

cards.term: Define electric current (steady and instantaneous).
cards.definition: Net charge crossing an area per unit time: I = q/t; in general \( I = \lim_{\Delta t\to0}\dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} \)

cards.term: Net charge q crossing an area when both + and − charges move?
cards.definition: q = q₊ − q₋ (forward flow of + minus forward flow of −); a negative I means current in the backward direction

cards.term: Orders of magnitude: lightning, domestic appliances, nerves?
cards.definition: Lightning: tens of thousands of A; appliances: ~1 A; nerves: μA

cards.term: Is current a scalar or a vector?
cards.definition: Scalar (the arrow only shows sense of flow; currents don’t add as vectors). \( I = \vec j\cdot\Delta\vec S \)

cards.term: Name natural free charges and the charge carriers in solids and electrolytes.
cards.definition: Free: ionosphere. Solid conductors: electrons (ions fixed). Electrolytes: positive and negative ions

cards.term: With no field, why is there no current even though electrons move fast?
cards.definition: Thermal motion is random: as many electrons cross each way, so the net flow is zero

cards.term: Charges ±Q stuck on the ends of a metal cylinder: what current flows?
cards.definition: Only a brief current until the charges are neutralised; a cell must replenish them to keep a steady field and current

cards.term: State Ohm’s law. Who, when?
cards.definition: \( V \propto I \), V = RI (at constant physical conditions); G. S. Ohm, 1828

cards.term: What analogy led Ohm to his law?
cards.definition: Heat conduction: electric field ↔ temperature gradient, current ↔ heat flow

cards.term: Resistance: unit and dimensions?
cards.definition: ohm, 1 Ω = 1 V A⁻¹; [ML²T⁻³A⁻²]

cards.term: How does R depend on length and area? Show why.
cards.definition: \( R = \rho\dfrac{l}{A} \): two slabs end to end double V at the same I (R ∝ l); cut lengthwise, each half carries I/2 at the same V (R ∝ 1/A)

cards.term: What is resistivity? Unit and dimensions?
cards.definition: Material constant ρ in R = ρl/A (depends on material and temperature, not size); Ω m, [ML³T⁻³A⁻²]

cards.term: Define current density. Unit?
cards.definition: \( j = I/A \) (area normal to the current), a vector along E; A m⁻²

cards.term: Ohm’s law in terms of E and j?
cards.definition: \( \vec E = \rho\,\vec j \) or \( \vec j = \sigma\vec E \), with conductivity σ = 1/ρ

cards.term: Correction: NCERT’s table gives the unit of conductivity σ as “S”. Right unit?
cards.definition: S m⁻¹ (siemens per metre) — the dimensions it lists, [M⁻¹L⁻³T³A²], are those of S m⁻¹; S alone is the unit of conductance (1/R)

cards.term: Points to ponder: is V = IR itself Ohm’s law?
cards.definition: No: V = IR defines R for any device. Ohm’s law is the claim that R is independent of V (I–V plot linear)

cards.term: Stretching trap: a wire is stretched to n times its length (volume constant). New R?
cards.definition: n²R: l → nl and A → A/n

cards.term: Acceleration of a free electron in a field E?
cards.definition: \( \vec a = -\dfrac{e\vec E}{m} \)

cards.term: Define relaxation time τ.
cards.definition: Average time between successive collisions of an electron

cards.term: Drift velocity formula?
cards.definition: \( \vec v_d = -\dfrac{e\vec E}{m}\tau \) — opposite to E for electrons

cards.term: Electrons accelerate, so why a constant drift velocity?
cards.definition: Each collision randomises the velocity; between collisions the gain is eEt/m, averaging to eEτ/m — like a ball bouncing down a pin-board

cards.term: Relation between current and drift speed?
cards.definition: \( I = neAv_d \) (charge in a cylinder of length v_d Δt crossing A per Δt)

cards.term: Identify: what does this path show?
cards.definition: Random zig-zag of an electron between collisions (A → B); with a field it ends at B′ — a slight drift opposite to E

cards.term: Derive conductivity from the drift model.
cards.definition: \( j = \dfrac{ne^2\tau}{m}E \Rightarrow \sigma = \dfrac{ne^2\tau}{m},\ \rho = \dfrac{m}{ne^2\tau} \) — Ohm’s law, if n and τ don’t depend on E

cards.term: Drift speed of electrons in copper (Example 3.1)
cards.definition: n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³; v_d = I/neA ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻³ m/s

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 3.1 · drift speed in copper

Find the missing step.

Cu wire, A = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ m², I = 1.5 A, ρ(density) = 9.0 × 10³ kg/m³, 63.5 u, one free electron per atom. v_d?
  1. n = (9.0 × 10⁶ g/m³ ÷ 63.5 g) × 6.0 × 10²³ = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³
  2. ?
  3. vd = 1.5/(8.5 × 10²⁸ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10⁻⁷) = 1.1 mm/s
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 3.1 · drift speed in copper

Find the missing step.

Cu wire, A = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ m², I = 1.5 A, ρ(density) = 9.0 × 10³ kg/m³, 63.5 u, one free electron per atom. v_d?
  1. n = (9.0 × 10⁶ g/m³ ÷ 63.5 g) × 6.0 × 10²³ = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³
  2. vd = I/(neA)
  3. vd = 1.5/(8.5 × 10²⁸ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10⁻⁷) = 1.1 mm/s

cards.term: Example 3.1(b): drift speed vs thermal speed of Cu atoms vs speed of the field signal?
cards.definition: v_d ~ 10⁻³ m/s; thermal speed of Cu atoms ~ 2 × 10² m/s (~10⁵ times more); field travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s (~10¹¹ times more)

cards.term: Update: how fast do the conduction electrons themselves move at random?
cards.definition: About 10⁶ m/s (the Fermi speed, a quantum effect) — so v_d is ~10⁻⁹ of their random speed; NCERT compares with atoms’ thermal speed instead

cards.term: Example 3.2(a): drift is only mm/s. Why does a bulb light instantly?
cards.definition: The electric field is set up in the whole circuit at nearly the speed of light; electrons everywhere start drifting at once

cards.term: Example 3.2(c): tiny drift, tiny charge — how are currents large?
cards.definition: The number density of free electrons is enormous, ~10²⁹ m⁻³

cards.term: Example 3.2(d): do all free electrons move in the same direction?
cards.definition: No: the small drift is superposed on large random velocities

cards.term: Example 3.2(e): are electron paths straight between collisions?
cards.definition: Without a field: straight. With a field: curved (parabolic), like projectiles

cards.term: Exercise 3.9: n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³, A = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m², I = 3.0 A. Time to drift along 3.0 m?
cards.definition: v_d ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻⁴ m/s → t ≈ 2.7 × 10⁴ s (~7.5 h)

cards.term: Define mobility. Unit?
cards.definition: \( \mu = \dfrac{|v_d|}{E} = \dfrac{e\tau}{m} \); m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ (1 m²/Vs = 10⁴ cm²/Vs); always positive

cards.term: Dimensions of mobility?
cards.definition: [M⁻¹ T² A]

cards.term: Mobile charge carriers in metals, ionised gases, electrolytes?
cards.definition: Metals: electrons; ionised gas: electrons and positive ions; electrolytes: positive and negative ions

cards.term: Teacher addition: conductivity in terms of mobility?
cards.definition: \( \sigma = ne\mu \)

cards.term: Three kinds of deviation from Ohm’s law?
cards.definition: (a) V not ∝ I (good conductor at large I); (b) depends on the sign of V (diode); (c) non-unique V for the same I (GaAs)

cards.term: Identify: what does this V–I graph show?
cards.definition: A good conductor deviating from the straight Ohm’s-law line (dashed) at large current

cards.term: Identify: which device has this I–V curve? Note the axes.
cards.definition: A diode: current depends on the sign of V; note different scales (mA/V forward, μA/V reverse)

cards.term: Identify: which material shows this I–V curve?
cards.definition: GaAs: a negative-resistance region, so one I can occur at more than one V

cards.term: Points to ponder: do silver or germanium obey Ohm’s law always?
cards.definition: Only within some range of field; all materials deviate in very strong fields

cards.term: Resistivity range of metals? Insulators?
cards.definition: Metals: 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ Ω m. Insulators (ceramic, rubber, plastic): ≥10¹⁸ times larger

cards.term: Note: NCERT’s summary says insulators are 10²² to 10²⁴ times more resistive; the text says 10¹⁸ or more. Which is right?
cards.definition: Both are rough: real insulators span ~10¹⁸–10²⁴ times metals (glass lower, hard rubber higher). Remember “metals 10⁻⁸, insulators ~10¹⁰ and up”

cards.term: Two special features of semiconductors’ resistivity?
cards.definition: It decreases with temperature, and falls sharply on adding small amounts of suitable impurities (doping)

cards.term: Resistivity of a metal vs temperature (limited range)?
cards.definition: \( \rho_T = \rho_0[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)] \); α > 0 for metals, unit K⁻¹ (or °C⁻¹)

cards.term: Define the temperature coefficient of resistivity α.
cards.definition: The fractional increase in resistivity per unit rise in temperature

cards.term: Identify: whose resistivity–temperature graph is this?
cards.definition: Copper: roughly linear near room temperature, curving away at low T

cards.term: Identify: whose resistivity–temperature graph is this? Why useful?
cards.definition: Nichrome: very weak dependence (also manganin, constantan) → used in standard resistors

cards.term: Identify: what kind of material has this ρ–T graph?
cards.definition: A semiconductor: ρ falls steeply as T rises

cards.term: Why does a metal’s resistivity rise with temperature?
cards.definition: n is almost constant, but faster random motion means more frequent collisions: τ decreases → ρ = m/ne²τ rises

cards.term: Why does a semiconductor’s resistivity fall with temperature?
cards.definition: n increases sharply with T, more than offsetting the fall in τ

cards.term: Nichrome is an alloy of which metals?
cards.definition: Nickel and chromium (NCERT adds iron, present in some grades)

cards.term: Heating element temperature from resistance (Example 3.3)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 3.3 · toaster

Find the missing step.

Nichrome element: 75.3 Ω at 27.0 °C; on 230 V the current settles at 2.68 A. α = 1.70 × 10⁻⁴ °C⁻¹. Steady temperature?
  1. Hot resistance R₂ = 230/2.68 = 85.8 Ω
  2. R₂ = R₁[1 + α(T₂ − T₁)]
  3. ?
  4. T₂ = 847 °C
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 3.3 · toaster

Find the missing step.

Nichrome element: 75.3 Ω at 27.0 °C; on 230 V the current settles at 2.68 A. α = 1.70 × 10⁻⁴ °C⁻¹. Steady temperature?
  1. Hot resistance R₂ = 230/2.68 = 85.8 Ω
  2. R₂ = R₁[1 + α(T₂ − T₁)]
  3. T₂ − T₁ = (85.8 − 75.3)/(75.3 × 1.70 × 10⁻⁴) = 820 °C
  4. T₂ = 847 °C

cards.term: Example 3.4: Pt thermometer reads 5 Ω at 0 °C, 5.23 Ω at 100 °C, 5.795 Ω in a bath. Bath temperature?
Exercise 3.3: 100 Ω at 27 °C becomes 117 Ω; α = 1.70 × 10⁻⁴ °C⁻¹. Temperature?
Exercise 3.5: silver wire 2.1 Ω at 27.5 °C, 2.7 Ω at 100 °C. α?
Exercise 3.6: nichrome on 230 V draws 3.2 A initially, 2.8 A steady; room 27 °C. Steady temperature?
cards.definition: R = 71.9 Ω → 82.1 Ω; ΔT ≈ 840 °C → ≈ 867 °C

cards.term: Exercise 3.4: 15 m wire, A = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m², R = 5.0 Ω. Resistivity?
cards.definition: ρ = RA/l = 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m

cards.term: Charge ΔQ falls through V: where does the lost potential energy go in a real conductor?
cards.definition: Not into KE (drift is steady) but into heat: collisions pass it to the ions, which vibrate more

cards.term: Power dissipated in a resistor?
cards.definition: \( P = IV = I^2R = \dfrac{V^2}{R} \) (ohmic loss)

cards.term: Who supplies the power in a simple cell–resistor circuit?
cards.definition: The chemical energy of the cell

cards.term: Why is power transmitted at very high voltage?
cards.definition: Line loss \( P_c = \dfrac{P^2R_c}{V^2} \) ∝ 1/V²: high V means small I and small loss; a transformer steps it down for use

cards.term: Series or parallel: which bulb glows brighter, 100 W or 60 W (both 220 V)?
cards.definition: Parallel: 100 W (P = V²/R, smaller R). Series: 60 W (same I, P = I²R, larger R)

cards.term: Define emf of a cell (in terms of electrode potentials).
cards.definition: ε = V₊ + V₋: potential difference between the terminals on open circuit (no current)

cards.term: Summary definition of emf (work).
cards.definition: Work done per unit charge by the source in taking charge from lower to higher potential energy inside it

cards.term: Is emf a force?
cards.definition: No: it is a potential difference; the name is historical

cards.term: Terminal voltage when the cell delivers current I?
cards.definition: \( V = \varepsilon - Ir \) (r = internal resistance)

cards.term: Current from a cell into an external resistor R?
cards.definition: \( I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R + r} \)

cards.term: Maximum current a cell can give? Is it safe?
cards.definition: \( I_{max} = \varepsilon/r \) (short circuit); usually far above the safe limit — damages the cell

cards.term: Terminal voltage while a cell is being charged?
cards.definition: \( V = \varepsilon + Ir \) (current enters at the + terminal)

cards.term: Which has higher internal resistance: dry cells or common electrolytic cells?
cards.definition: Dry cells (much higher)

cards.term: Exercise 3.1: car battery ε = 12 V, r = 0.4 Ω. Maximum current?
cards.definition: 30 A

cards.term: Exercise 3.2: ε = 10 V, r = 3 Ω, I = 0.5 A. External R and terminal voltage?
cards.definition: R = 20 − 3 = 17 Ω; V = 10 − 1.5 = 8.5 V

cards.term: Terminal voltage during charging (Exercise 3.8)
cards.definition: I = 7 A; V = ε + Ir = 11.5 V; the series resistor limits the current

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Exercise 3.8 · charging a battery

Find the missing step.

8.0 V battery (r = 0.5 Ω) charged from 120 V dc through a 15.5 Ω series resistor. Terminal voltage?
  1. Net driving emf = 120 − 8 = 112 V
  2. I = 112/(15.5 + 0.5) = 7 A
  3. ?
  4. The series resistor limits the current, which would otherwise be dangerously large
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Exercise 3.8 · charging a battery

Find the missing step.

8.0 V battery (r = 0.5 Ω) charged from 120 V dc through a 15.5 Ω series resistor. Terminal voltage?
  1. Net driving emf = 120 − 8 = 112 V
  2. I = 112/(15.5 + 0.5) = 7 A
  3. Charging: V = ε + Ir = 8 + 7 × 0.5 = 11.5 V
  4. The series resistor limits the current, which would otherwise be dangerously large

cards.term: Teacher addition: power delivered to R by a cell (ε, r) is maximum when?
cards.definition: \( R = r \) (maximum power transfer); P_max = ε²/4r

cards.term: Two cells in series (+ to −): equivalent emf and internal resistance?
cards.definition: \( \varepsilon_{eq} = \varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2,\ r_{eq} = r_1 + r_2 \)

cards.term: Two cells in series with like terminals joined (opposing)?
cards.definition: \( \varepsilon_{eq} = \varepsilon_1 - \varepsilon_2 \) (ε₁ > ε₂); r still adds

cards.term: Two cells in parallel: equivalent emf and internal resistance?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{1}{r_{eq}} = \dfrac1{r_1} + \dfrac1{r_2},\quad \dfrac{\varepsilon_{eq}}{r_{eq}} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_1}{r_1} + \dfrac{\varepsilon_2}{r_2} \)

cards.term: Parallel cells with one reversed?
cards.definition: Use the same formulas with \( \varepsilon_2 \to -\varepsilon_2 \)

cards.term: Teacher addition: n identical cells (ε, r) in parallel?
cards.definition: ε_eq = ε, r_eq = r/n: same emf, more current capacity

cards.term: Teacher addition: when is series better, when parallel (n identical cells, external R)?
cards.definition: Series if R ≫ r (I = nε/(R + nr)); parallel if R ≪ r (I = ε/(R + r/n))

cards.term: State Kirchhoff’s junction rule. Basis?
cards.definition: Sum of currents entering = sum leaving; based on conservation of charge (no charge piles up in steady state)

cards.term: State Kirchhoff’s loop rule. Basis?
cards.definition: Algebraic sum of potential changes around any closed loop = 0; based on potential being single-valued (energy conservation)

cards.term: Identify: write the junction rule at a and the loop rules shown.
cards.definition: I₃ = I₁ + I₂; loop ahdcba: −30I₁ − 41I₃ + 45 = 0; loop ahdefga: −30I₁ + 21I₂ − 80 = 0

cards.term: Sign convention: crossing a resistor and a cell in a loop?
cards.definition: Resistor along the current: −IR (drop); against: +IR. Cell from − to +: +ε; from + to −: −ε

cards.term: A current comes out negative after solving. What does it mean?
cards.definition: The actual current flows opposite to the arrow you assumed — no need to redo

cards.term: Points to ponder: does bending or reorienting wires affect the junction rule?
cards.definition: No: it is charge conservation, independent of geometry

cards.term: Cube of equal resistors, body diagonal (Example 3.5)
cards.definition: R_eq = 5R/6; with 10 V and R = 1 Ω: 12 A total, 4 A in each edge next to A or C′, 2 A in the middle edges

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 3.5 · cube of resistors

Find the missing step.

Twelve 1 Ω resistors on the edges of a cube; 10 V across diagonally opposite corners A and C′. R_eq and currents?
  1. By symmetry each of the 3 edges from A carries I, total 3I
  2. Each splits into two edges carrying I/2, which recombine into 3 edges carrying I
  3. ?
  4. Req = ε/3I = 5R/6 = 5/6 Ω; 3I = 12 A, I = 4 A
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 3.5 · cube of resistors

Find the missing step.

Twelve 1 Ω resistors on the edges of a cube; 10 V across diagonally opposite corners A and C′. R_eq and currents?
  1. By symmetry each of the 3 edges from A carries I, total 3I
  2. Each splits into two edges carrying I/2, which recombine into 3 edges carrying I
  3. Loop A → B → C → C′ → battery: ε = IR + ½IR + IR = (5/2) IR
  4. Req = ε/3I = 5R/6 = 5/6 Ω; 3I = 12 A, I = 4 A

cards.term: Identify: equivalent resistance between opposite corners of this cube (each edge R)?
cards.definition: \( R_{eq} = \dfrac56 R \) (symmetry: I, I/2, I pattern)

cards.term: Teacher addition: cube of resistors R between the ends of one edge? Across a face diagonal?
cards.definition: Edge: 7R/12; face diagonal: 3R/4; body diagonal: 5R/6

cards.term: Example 3.6 (Fig 3.17): branch currents?
cards.definition: I₁ = 2.5 A, I₂ = 5/8 A, I₃ = 15/8 A; AB 5/8 A, CA and BC 2.5 A, AD and DEB 15/8 A, CD 0

cards.term: Correction/reading note: NCERT prints I₃ in Example 3.6 as a mixed fraction. Value?
cards.definition: I₃ = 1⁷⁄₈ A = 15/8 A = 1.875 A (check: I₂ + I₃ = 2.5 A)

cards.term: Wheatstone bridge: name the arms.
cards.definition: Battery across A–C (battery arm); galvanometer across B–D (galvanometer arm); four resistors R₁…R₄

cards.term: Balance condition of a Wheatstone bridge?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{R_2}{R_1} = \dfrac{R_4}{R_3} \) → I_g = 0 (null deflection)

cards.term: How is an unknown resistance found with a Wheatstone bridge?
cards.definition: Put it in arm 4, fix R₁ and R₂, vary R₃ until null: \( R_4 = R_3\dfrac{R_2}{R_1} \)

cards.term: At balance, does it matter if the battery and galvanometer are swapped?
cards.definition: No: the balance condition is unchanged; the galvanometer resistance also doesn’t matter at balance

cards.term: Name a practical device based on the Wheatstone bridge.
cards.definition: The meter bridge

cards.term: Mnemonic: balance condition?
cards.definition: “Products of opposite arms are equal”: R₁R₄ = R₂R₃

cards.term: Current through the galvanometer in an unbalanced bridge (Example 3.7)
cards.definition: Three loop equations; I₂ = 31.5 I_g; I_g ≈ 4.87 mA

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 3.7 · unbalanced bridge

Find the missing step.

AB = 100 Ω, BC = 10 Ω, CD = 5 Ω, DA = 60 Ω; galvanometer 15 Ω across BD; 10 V across AC. I_g?
  1. Loop BADB: 100I₁ + 15Ig − 60I₂ = 0
  2. ?
  3. Loop ADCEA: 60I₂ + 5(I₂ + Ig) = 10
  4. Eliminate I₁: I₂ = 31.5 Ig → Ig = 2/410.5 = 4.87 mA
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 3.7 · unbalanced bridge

Find the missing step.

AB = 100 Ω, BC = 10 Ω, CD = 5 Ω, DA = 60 Ω; galvanometer 15 Ω across BD; 10 V across AC. I_g?
  1. Loop BADB: 100I₁ + 15Ig − 60I₂ = 0
  2. Loop BCDB: 10(I₁ − Ig) − 15Ig − 5(I₂ + Ig) = 0
  3. Loop ADCEA: 60I₂ + 5(I₂ + Ig) = 10
  4. Eliminate I₁: I₂ = 31.5 Ig → Ig = 2/410.5 = 4.87 mA

cards.term: Identify: the unbalanced bridge of Example 3.7. Why is it unbalanced?
Exercise 3.7 (Fig 3.20): currents in the network with 10 V and a 10 Ω series resistor?
cards.definition: R_AC = 7 Ω → total 10/17 A; AB and DC 4/17 A, AD and BC 6/17 A, BD 2/17 A (from D to B)

cards.term: Points to ponder: why can j = ρv (charge density × velocity) not be applied to the total charge of a wire?
cards.definition: A current-carrying wire is neutral (ρ₊ = −ρ₋, total ρ = 0), yet j ≠ 0; apply j = ρv to each carrier type separately (j = ρ₋v₋, as v₊ ≈ 0)

cards.term: Kirchhoff’s rules: which conservation law does each express?
cards.definition: Junction: charge. Loop: energy (potential is single-valued)

cards.term: Chapter 3 formula sheet
cards.definition: Resistance: R = ρl/A; Drift velocity: v_d = eEτ/m; Current: I = neAv_d; Resistivity: ρ = m/ne²τ; Mobility: μ = v_d/E = eτ/m; Temperature: ρ_T = ρ₀[1 + α(T − T₀)]; Cell: V = ε − Ir, I = ε/(R + r); Power: P = VI = I²R = V²/R; Bridge balance: R₁R₄ = R₂R₃
